decision_context: A high-rise factory employs a large, economically dependent workforce among substantial combustible production material. Management has legitimate concerns about theft, unauthorised departure and production control. Exit doors have locks, but the supplied inspection account found them unlocked during its visit. Routine door status, individual knowledge and the completeness of fire protection remain uncertain. Management must decide whether property/production controls may compromise emergency egress or whether worker escape and fire protection take priority.
decision_question: Should the factory maintain access-control and low-cost safety arrangements that can obstruct emergency escape, or redesign security and production controls so every worker has rapid unobstructed egress and stronger fire protection?
available_actions: Maintain current access-control practices, including locking or tightly controlling selected exits during work to prevent theft/unauthorised departure, while relying on existing escape/fire-response arrangements.
Keep every required emergency exit readily openable from inside during occupancy while using guards/checks or other non-blocking theft controls.
Add regular drills, marked escape routes and assigned responsibility for verifying exits remain usable throughout each shift.
Install stronger fire protection where technically feasible.
Reduce combustible accumulation/crowding and review whether escape capacity can evacuate the workforce safely.

affected_parties.party: Factory workers with low bargaining power
affected_parties.known_interests_or_risks: Life, bodily safety, evacuation, income and freedom from being trapped by workplace-control systems during emergency.
Property protection, production continuity, labour discipline, cost of safety improvements and business responsibility.
Loss of income, caregiving and family members if workers are killed/injured.
Fire spread, rescue burden and safety during an industrial fire.
Enforcing life-safety rules and responsibility for foreseeable high-rise workplace hazards.

known_evidence.claim: The factory is high above ground, holds a large workforce and contains substantial combustible production material.
A serious fire can develop quickly and makes evacuation capacity/time life-critical.

Theft and unauthorised departure are management concerns. Guards or checks that leave emergency exits openable are proposed alternatives; their effectiveness and cost have not been established for this factory.

An inspector reports that stairway exit doors had locks but were unlocked when inspected during work. This observation does not establish routine locking practices, the status of every exit on other shifts, or what any particular manager knew.
The supplied account identifies fire pails and a hose among the factory protections. It does not establish a complete installation inventory or routine readiness of this equipment.
When only a small number of evacuation routes serve a large workforce, failure or obstruction of one route can sharply reduce escape capacity.
Workers rely on employment and have little practical power individually to redesign exits, install suppression systems or override management security policy.

Keeping exits openable and using non-blocking security controls are physically distinct measures. Whether particular guards or checks would meet security needs at an acceptable cost remains uncertain.
Safety upgrades impose business costs while catastrophic risk from inadequate protection falls primarily on workers.

known_uncertainties: Exact probability/timing of a serious fire.
Precise day-to-day exit-control practice and who knows each door's status.
Which measures are legally mandatory versus morally prudent.

Whether automatic sprinkler protection is installed; the supplied installation evidence does not settle this. The selected action describes a locking/control policy whose routine operation is not established by the single inspection.
known_alternatives: Unlocked/openable emergency egress plus non-blocking security controls.
Drills, exit checks and named supervisory responsibility.
Reduced combustible accumulation/crowding and verified escape capacity.
Independent safety inspection and corrective deadlines.
requested_output: Separate theft/attendance objectives from the means used to control exits.
Assess whether cost/property benefits are obtained by exporting safety risk to low-power workers.
Do not treat employment as consent to avoidable lethal hazards.
Compare less dangerous means achieving the same business purpose.
Assess employer and regulator duties without inventing personal criminal intent.
Give a Moral Code assessment without identifying the historical case or using its later death toll.
